extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists and students interested in IOC governance and Olympic policy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the International Olympic Committee's stated mission, membership rules, hosting/bid requirements, revenue distribution policies, athlete eligibility and ethics standards, and other governance criteria that guide IOC decisions and operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote ethics and good governance in sport
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support the promotion of ethics and good governance in sport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the first item of the IOC's mission; implies supporting governance reforms, anti-corruption measures, transparency and ethical conduct across the Olympic Movement. No numeric scoring guidance provided; context includes later references to reforms after bid scandals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support education of youth through sport
rubrics_metrics.description: To support the education of youth through sport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the IOC mission; encompasses programmes such as Olympic education and collaboration with institutions like the International Olympic Academy (IOA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure spirit of fair play and avoid violence
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure that the spirit of fair play prevails and violence is avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a mission objective guiding conduct of athletes, officials and organizers; ties into anti-doping, safe-sport, and disciplinary frameworks mentioned elsewhere in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage and support organisation, development and coordination of sport
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support the organisation, development, and coordination of sport and sports competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad mandate to assist National Olympic Committees, International Federations, and Organising Committees in developing and coordinating events and programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure regular celebration of the Olympic Games
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure the regular celebration of the Olympic Games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational requirement underpinning IOC scheduling and the four-year cycle; relates to decisions about postponement/cancellation (e.g., COVID-19 postponement noted historically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperate with competent organisations to place sport at the service of humanity and promote peace
rubrics_metrics.description: To cooperate with competent public or private organisations and authorities endeavouring to place sport at the service of humanity and thereby to promote peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets expectation of intergovernmental and NGO collaboration (example: IOC Permanent Observer status at the UN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen unity, independence, political neutrality and autonomy of the Olympic Movement
rubrics_metrics.description: To take action to strengthen the unity, independence, political neutrality, and autonomy of the Olympic Movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core governance principle; invoked in discussions about boycotts, host-country human-rights controversies and the IOC's stance on not politicising the Games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support elected athlete representatives via the IOC Athletes' Commission
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support elected representatives of athletes, working with the IOC Athletes' Commission as their official representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance criterion to ensure athlete representation in IOC decision-making; resulted in the creation and empowerment of an Athletes' Commission with provisional athlete membership in some reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote women in sport and pursue equality
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support the promotion of women in sport in pursuit of equality between men and women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objective that informs gender-equality initiatives, event inclusion decisions, and governance representation targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect clean athletes and integrity of sport (anti-doping and anti-manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To protect clean athletes and the integrity of sport, by leading the fight against doping, and by taking action against all forms of manipulation of competitions and related corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encompasses coordination with WADA and disciplinary processes; historical examples include Russian doping scandals and the IOC's role in reinstatement/sanctions. Guidance includes that IOC leads anti-doping policy and funding partnerships with anti-doping bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage measures relating to medical care and health of athletes
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support measures relating to the medical care and health of athletes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers policies such as pandemic risk mitigation (examples: event-specific FIE risk mitigation documents) and athlete medical care provisions; no numeric targets given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose political or commercial abuse of sport and athletes
rubrics_metrics.description: To oppose any political or commercial abuse of sport and athletes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle that influences IOC responses to host-country human-rights concerns, diplomatic boycotts, and restrictions on commercial exploitation. Appears alongside the requirement that IOC members act independently of commercial and political interests (see member oath).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support social and professional future of athletes
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support the efforts of sports organisations and public authorities to provide for the social and professional future of athletes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy aim for athlete career programmes and Olympic Solidarity support for NOCs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage development of sport for all
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support the development of sport for all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusive-development principle guiding outreach and funding programmes (e.g., Olympic Solidarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental responsibility and sustainable development in sport and Games operations
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support a responsible concern for environmental issues, to promote sustainable development in sport and to require that the Olympic Games are operated accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented via candidate/host-city requirements, the IOC Sustainability and Legacy Commission, detailed sustainability frameworks (e.g., for PyeongChang 2018 and Tokyo 2020) and specific venue-construction and air/water/soil mitigation measures. Examples: Beijing 2008 'Green Olympics' projects, candidate-city environmental impact information, and the obligation for host cities to provide a comprehensive environmental strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote a positive legacy for host cities, regions and countries
rubrics_metrics.description: To promote a positive legacy from the Olympic Games to the host cities, regions and countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Influences venue legacy planning, remediation (e.g., Homebush Bay soil remediation), and post-Games use commitments; related to sustainability and community impact promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend sport with culture and education and support Olympic education institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage and support initiatives blending sport with culture and education; to encourage and support the activities of the International Olympic Academy and other institutions which dedicate themselves to Olympic education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers cultural/educational programming and partnerships, and support for academic/educational institutions focusing on Olympism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote safe sport and protect athletes from harassment and abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: To promote safe sport and the protection of athletes from all forms of harassment and abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy priority in the mission; linked to disciplinary and safeguarding frameworks, and referenced in modern governance changes to protect athletes' welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: IOC member oath / conduct obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: "I will respect the Olympic Charter and accept the decisions of the IOC. I will always act independently of commercial and political interests as well as of any racial or religious consideration. I will fully comply with the IOC Code of Ethics. I promise to fight against all forms of discrimination and dedicate myself in all circumstances to promote the interests of the International Olympic Committee and Olympic Movement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All IOC members must swear to this oath; it functions as a binding statement of ethics and independence. Breach of the oath can lead to expulsion or sanctions as noted in membership cessation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership cap and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of all serving IOC members may not exceed 115. Categories include athlete representatives (IOC Athletes' Commission), representatives from International Federations, representatives from National Olympic Committees, and individual members not linked to specific organisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines composition limits and categories for membership. Practical implications for elections and representation; membership numbers and categories are enforced by the Olympic Charter and Session decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership cessation conditions (resignation, non-re-election, age, attendance, domicile, role-change, expulsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership ends by resignation, non-re-election, reaching age limits (end of calendar year when members reach 70 or 80 depending on their join period), failure to attend sessions or take active part for two consecutive years, transfer of domicile/main interest away from original country, ceasing to hold the function they held at election (for certain role-linked members), or expulsion for betraying the oath or knowingly jeopardising IOC interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age-rule detail: members who joined in the 1900s cease at age 80; those who joined in the 2000s cease at age 70. Expulsion requires a Session decision and is used for serious breaches. Attendance and activity requirements create an accountability mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: IOC Session powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC Session is the general meeting (supreme organ) and may adopt or amend the Olympic Charter; elect IOC members, honorary members, the President, vice-presidents and other Executive Board members; and elect the host city of the Olympic Games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Session is held once a year and decisions are final. Extraordinary Sessions may be convened as specified (see convening rules). These powers set the procedural framework for major governance actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: IOC Session convening rules (ordinary and extraordinary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC Session is held once a year; Extraordinary Sessions may be convened by the President or upon the written request of at least one-third of the members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines thresholds and authorities for calling meetings that can make binding governance decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host-city environmental and sustainability requirements for bidding
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC requires cities bidding to host the Olympics to provide a comprehensive strategy to protect the environment in preparation for hosting, and following the conclusion of the Games. Every candidate city must provide information on environmental health issues such as air quality and environmental impact assessments; host cities may declare 'pledges' to address specific environmental concerns; every host city must collaborate with the United Nations on environmental objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented through the IOC Sustainability and Legacy Commission and through detailed frameworks for specific Games (examples: Beijing 2008, PyeongChang 2018, Tokyo 2020). Candidate-city submissions must include assessments and mitigation plans for air, water and soil impacts; failure to address these concerns can weigh against a bid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue construction and environmental mitigation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue construction plans must consider effects on air, soil and water; primary mitigation measures include traffic control, emission standards for vehicles, dust control on sites, relocation/closure of polluting plants, and remediation of contaminated soils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Beijing 2008 measures (vehicle bans, odd-even rules, industrial plant relocation, furnace replacement, coal-to-gas replacements), Sydney 2000 soil remediation at Homebush Bay, and traffic-control measures recommended generally. Guidance appears as best-practice examples rather than prescriptive formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue sources and distribution framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Olympic Movement generates revenue through five major programmes: broadcast partnerships, commercial sponsorship (TOP programme), domestic sponsorship (OCOGs), ticketing, and licensing within host countries. The IOC distributes revenue to organisations throughout the Olympic Movement to support staging of the Games and sport development; the IOC retains approximately 10% of Olympic marketing revenue for operational and administrative costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 2013–2016, 73% of IOC revenue was from broadcasting and 18% from Olympic Partners. Specific distribution examples: TOP programme revenue is shared between OCOGs in a quadrennium (approximately 50% of TOP value-in-kind and cash shared between two OCOGs; about 30% to summer OCOG and 20% to winter OCOG). Broadcast revenue: the IOC contributes 49% of Olympic broadcast revenue for each Games to the OCOG. Historical figures (Rio 2016, Sochi 2014) are given as examples of amounts received by OCOGs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and funding to NOCs, IFs and other organisations
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC distributes TOP programme revenue and broadcast revenue to National Olympic Committees (NOCs), International Olympic Sports Federations (IOSFs/IFs), Olympic Solidarity and other recognised international sports organisations (including IPC and WADA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides financial support to NOCs (example: ~US$318.5 million for 2001–2004 quadrennium) and IFs (examples of broadcast revenue shares for winter sports IFs). IOC is the largest revenue source for many IOSFs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-corruption, gift limits and bid-process safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: After bid scandals (e.g., Salt Lake 2002), stricter rules were adopted for future bids: caps were placed on how much IOC members could accept from bid cities; new term and age limits for IOC membership were introduced; an Athletes' Commission was created and some former athletes were given provisional membership status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context: investigations into gift-taking led to expulsions and sanctions and to structural reforms intended to reduce corruption and conflicts of interest. Guidance implies strict limits on gifts/entertainment and heightened transparency in bid processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olympic honors criteria (medals and awards)
rubrics_metrics.description: IOC awards gold, silver and bronze medals for top competitors and other honours with stated criteria: Pierre de Coubertin Medal (athletes who demonstrate a special spirit of sportsmanship), Olympic Cup (institutions/associations with a record of merit and integrity in developing the Olympic Movement), Olympic Order (individuals for exceptionally distinguished contributions), Olympic Laurel (individuals who promote education, culture, development, and peace through sport), Olympic town status (towns important to the Olympic Movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each honour has its own purpose-driven criterion; examples are given directly in the article. These awards serve as recognition criteria rather than performance/scoring metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex verification / hyperandrogenism and athlete eligibility rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, the IOC has implemented sex-verification policies (from Barr body tests to PCR testing and testosterone-based regulations). By 2011 the IOC had a Hyperandrogenism Regulation aiming to standardise natural testosterone levels in women athletes; athletes exceeding thresholds could be prohibited from competing until medical treatment adjusted levels. Policies have been contested, suspended (e.g., following appeals to the Court of Arbitration for Sport), and evolved over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides the historical evolution, named cases (Martínez-Patiño, Semenya, Dutee Chand, etc.), and notes controversies including disproportionate impact on certain ethnicities. The regulation is an eligibility criterion applied case-by-case and has been subject to suspension and legal challenge; guidance here is descriptive rather than technical threshold numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that Olympic Games must not be politicised
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC has stated that 'the Olympic Games must not be politicised' in response to political/human-rights criticisms of certain host bids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the IOC in responses to calls for boycotts or political pressure on host selection; in practice this principle interacts with other mission items (neutrality, human-rights considerations) and has been a point of controversy when human-rights groups pressure the IOC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate/host-city obligations on environmental health information
rubrics_metrics.description: Every candidate city must provide information on environmental health issues such as air quality and environmental impact assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of bid evaluation; candidate submissions must include environmental assessments and mitigation plans (air quality, PM2.5/PM10 concerns, runoff and water impacts). Examples given include monitoring and mitigation programmes at Beijing 2008.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traffic control as primary air-quality mitigation during Games
rubrics_metrics.description: Traffic control is identified as the primary method to reduce concentrations of air pollutants during and after venue construction and to improve air quality during the Games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vehicle bans, odd-even licence plate rules, restricting heavy vehicles near venues; provided as a recommended mitigation approach based on Beijing and other host experiences.
